passage:
Deepak: hey, are you free at 8 tonight? want to sort out the dishes and the wifi bill. not an angry thing, promise
Mahima: sure. what's up?
Deepak: i've washed the dishes 5 days in a row and the wifi share is due. could we make a chore chart? i'll draw it up
Mahima: fair. exams have flattened me this week. can we do alternate days and i pay the wifi by friday?
Deepak: that works. thank you for hearing me 🙂
Mahima: thanks for asking nicely instead of leaving a note on the fridge 😅
Deepak: haha. see you at 8

qa.q: How many days in a row had Deepak washed the dishes?
qa.a: Deepak had washed the dishes 5 days in a row.

qa.q: Why did Deepak ask to talk at eight and say it was not an angry thing?
qa.a: Deepak wanted a calm moment to sort things out, so that Mahima would not feel attacked.

qa.q: What made the plan easy to agree on?
qa.a: Deepak gave specifics and a proposed fix, and Mahima could add a limit of Mahima's own, alternate days because of exams.

qa.q: How might Mahima have felt on seeing the first message?
qa.a: Mahima may have been a little worried at first, but the friendly tone and the promise of no anger made it easy to answer fairly.

grounding: A roommate raises broken agreements at a calm time with specifics and a proposed fix instead of a passive-aggressive note.

passage:
In their rented room behind the Sirsa bus depot, Vikas and his cousin Simran had one rule for the first term: whoever was up first filled the water drums before the tank ran dry at seven.

By October it was always Vikas. Three mornings in a row he hauled buckets while Simran slept. He started banging the steel mugs loudly and sighing. Simran just rolled over.

On Sunday afternoon, when they were both eating jalebi on the roof and nobody was in a hurry, Vikas said, "Can I bring up the water thing? This week I filled the drums Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday. I'm getting angry, and I don't want to."

Simran winced. "My alarm doesn't work before six."

"Then how about this: I do mornings, you do the evening dishes and the gas cylinder booking?"

Simran thought about it. "Deal. And I'll stop leaving pans overnight."

The mugs have been quiet since.

qa.q: When did the tank run dry?
qa.a: The tank ran dry at seven.

qa.q: What was Vikas feeling when he banged the steel mugs and sighed?
qa.a: Vikas felt frustrated and resentful about doing the water duty alone, and was showing it indirectly.

qa.q: Which choice worked better than banging mugs, and why?
qa.a: Raising it on a calm Sunday with specific days and a proposed swap worked, because Simran could respond to facts and a fair fix instead of noise.

qa.q: How does Simran probably feel when Vikas names the specific days?
qa.a: Simran likely feels a little guilty and caught out, but not attacked, so she explains her alarm and agrees to the swap.

grounding: Shows a roommate raising broken agreements at a calm time with specifics and a proposed fix instead of passive-aggressive signals.

passage:
The sticky note on the fridge in the Cape Town student flat read, in Lindiwe's handwriting: "Some of us have exams. Just saying."

Jin's boyfriend had stayed over five nights out of seven, although they had agreed on two. Lindiwe had written three notes that month. Jin had answered none of them, only started leaving earlier.

On Saturday morning, over toast, Lindiwe pulled the notes off the fridge. "I'm sorry about these. They weren't fair. Can we talk properly?"

Jin put down her mug. "Okay."

"We said two nights a week. It's been five most weeks this month. I can't study in the lounge, and the bathroom's always busy at seven."

"I didn't realise it was that many," Jin said slowly.

"What if we use a shared calendar? Two nights, and you tell me a day before. And exam weeks, none."

Jin nodded. "That's fair. I'll tell him tonight."

qa.q: How many nights had Jin's boyfriend been staying over, and how many had they agreed on?
qa.a: He had stayed five nights out of seven, although they had agreed on two.

qa.q: Why did Lindiwe apologise for the sticky notes?
qa.a: Lindiwe felt uncomfortable and a bit ashamed of them, seeing that passive-aggressive notes were unfair and had not solved anything.

qa.q: What made the Saturday conversation work?
qa.a: Lindiwe chose a calm time, gave specific facts about nights and effects, and proposed a clear fix with a shared calendar.

qa.q: How might Jin have felt reading the notes compared with the Saturday talk?
qa.a: The notes probably made Jin feel judged and avoidant, while the direct talk let Jin understand the problem and agree to a fix.

grounding: Shows a roommate moving from passive-aggressive notes to raising the broken agreement calmly with specifics and a proposed fix.
